children: The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana said on Wednesday that any parties appearing in the district must disclose details about their use of third-party litigation financing, adding to a small but growing patchwork of similar transparency rules in the federal courts.
The court in a new standing order said parties are required to disclose the name and address of all litigation funders backing their cases.
Third-party funders agree to finance litigation in exchange for a cut of an eventual settlement or judgment.

The Louisiana federal court's order does not require parties to fully disclose funding agreements, but the parties must give a brief description of the agreement and state whether a funder has "any right to approve or influence litigation decisions, including settlement decisions."
The order gives parties 14 days to comply with the disclosure requirement, starting when they enter a case or when a funding agreement is signed.
A spokesperson for the International Legal Finance Association, a trade group representing litigation funders in the U.S., did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Louisiana federal court's standing order is the latest in an emerging wave of federal court orders and state laws requiring disclosure of third-party financing agreements.

Bills introduced by Republican lawmakers in the U.S. House and Senate that would mandate disclosure of litigation financing agreements nationwide have so far failed to gain any traction in Congress. The bills face opposition from both Democratic lawmakers and conservative groups
In October 2024, a federal judicial rules-making panel said it would study whether a nationwide rule requiring disclosure of third-party litigation funding in lawsuits is necessary.
